chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Hassan, from Abu Muhammad al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, from Ali (peace be upon him), who said:

One prayer in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) is equivalent to a thousand prayers, and one prayer in al-Masjid al-A'zam (Mecca) is equivalent to one hundred prayers, and one prayer in the mosque of the tribe is equivalent to twenty-five prayers, and one prayer in the market mosque is equivalent to twelve prayers, and a man's prayer in his own house alone is equivalent to one prayer.

key_terms.الْمَسْجِدُ الْأَعْظَمُ: Al-Masjid al-A'zam (The Greatest Mosque, i.e., Masjid al-Haram in Mecca)
key_terms.بَيْتُ الْمَقْدِسِ: Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), a highly virtuous place for prayer
key_terms.صَلَاةٌ: Prayer (salat), the act of worship being evaluated for reward
key_terms.مَسْجِدُ السُّوقِ: Market mosque, a smaller place of prayer in commercial areas
key_terms.مَسْجِدُ الْقَبِيلَةِ: Mosque of the tribe, referring to the main mosque of a local community or tribe

ai.seo_question: What is the reward multiplier for praying in Jerusalem, Mecca, and local mosques compared to praying at home?
ai.summary: This hadith from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* establishes a graded hierarchy of spiritual merit for prayers based on location, reflecting the historical significance of Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis) as the first Qibla and the enduring centrality of Mecca. It underscores the Shia scholarly view that while communal prayer in local mosques holds value, the sanctity of specific holy sites amplifies the reward, yet individual devotion at home remains valid and distinct.
